beats.say: This beetle got swallowed by a toad. And the toad threw it back up, alive.
The bombardier beetle. It fights back with boiling hot spray.
A hungry toad spotted one, and gulped it down.
But inside the toad's belly, the beetle fired its spray.
Scientists in Japan fed these beetles to toads, to see what happens.
Twelve minutes to almost two hours later, the toad threw up.
Out came the beetle. Alive, and it walked away.
It got eaten, and it still won.
Almost half the swallowed beetles escaped like that.
Beetles that had already used up their spray almost never got out.
So how does the spray work? In its rear, it keeps two chemicals.
When it's grabbed, it squirts them into a tough little chamber, with enzymes.
They react, and the spray comes out at about boiling, one hundred degrees.
It's not one blast. It fires hundreds of tiny pops every second.
You can even hear it go pop.
And it can aim. It swings its rear end to hit whatever grabbed it.
On your fingers, it stings, stains your skin, and stinks.
Would you pick one up with your bare hands?
Swallowed, set off a bomb in a toad's stomach, and walked out.
Follow me. Next, a bug that never stops growing.
